Oracle is pushing ahead with heavy AI infrastructure spending, backed by a US$664b cloud backlog and strong Oracle Cloud Infrastructure growth, while funding a large portion through customer prepayments, supplier financing and planned debt raises.

Rising credit default swap spreads, record borrowing costs and delays around Project Jupiter and related power infrastructure put Oracle's execution risk and free cash flow strain in sharp focus, even as it rolls out AI-first offerings like NetSuite QuickStart and deepens cloud security collaborations.

We will look at how Oracle's investment narrative holds up when aggressive AI data center CapEx meets rising funding and execution risk.

Spot opportunities beyond Oracle by scanning hand picked 55 AI infrastructure stocks that are riding the same AI data center and cloud infrastructure wave, which is now under intense funding and execution scrutiny.

Oracle Investment Narrative Recap

To own Oracle today, you need to believe the firm can turn its large AI cloud backlog into profitable usage while absorbing heavy near-term spending and higher funding costs. The key short-term swing factor is execution on AI capacity, including Project Jupiter and other data centers, so that GPU and data center utilization stays tight against US$664 billion of remaining obligations.

The biggest risk is that AI infrastructure build accelerates faster than actual workloads. This scenario could leave Oracle with cash burn, higher interest expenses and credit concerns before contracts ramp. Recent security, marketplace and client wins are helpful for the story, but they do not yet change the fact that execution and free cash flow timing remain the primary pressure points.

The Marvell, Microsoft and Oracle hardware security module working group inside the Open Compute Project is the announcement that most directly intersects with the current AI buildout narrative. It ties Oracle's infrastructure plan to a push for standardized, FIPS 140-3 Level 3 security at the server layer. This matters if customers are signing multi-year AI contracts that expect tight key management.

For investors, this HSM effort feeds into the same catalyst that underpins the broader thesis. Oracle is attempting to position OCI as both high performance and highly secure for AI workloads, from OpenAI-scale tenants to large enterprises. That supports the idea that the large backlog can be used efficiently, while still leaving funding structure, interest costs and project timing as the main operational watchpoints.

When investors think about cloud computing, Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOGL)(NASDAQ: GOOG) and Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) are often the first names that come to mind. But Oracle (NYSE: ORCL) is also making a strong push into AI infrastructure, and its rapidly growing cloud business offers another way to ride the AI boom.

With $5,000 to put to work today, investors may find Oracle a more compelling cloud choice than either of those giants. The reason starts with how fast its cloud business is growing.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
This database giant is becoming a major force in AI cloud

Oracle may be best known for its database software, which businesses use to store and manage critical information. These days, that established business is laying the foundation for a much bigger opportunity: supplying the cloud infrastructure that other companies need to develop and run AI models.

Oracle's cloud infrastructure business is already seeing solid growth, with revenue climbing 121% to $7.4 billion in its most recent quarter. That suggests its cloud business is becoming an important growth engine rather than simply an extension of its traditional software business.

Its massive backlog, meanwhile, provides a longer runway for growth. Oracle's remaining performance obligations (RPO) reached a record $664 billion, up $209 billion year over year. RPO represents contracted revenue that has not yet been recognized, giving investors a clearer view of the company's future revenue.

That means Oracle is seeing surging demand from customers that need cloud capacity for AI training, applications, and inference. Still, that demand isn't limited to one type of customer, and Oracle is positioning itself to capture several parts of that market.

But with competition picking up, the next question is how Oracle is setting itself apart from the biggest names in the cloud business.

Oracle has a different advantage from its larger cloud rivals

Microsoft Azure and Alphabet's Google Cloud compete across broad cloud ecosystems. However, Oracle's opportunity is somewhat different: it has the luxury of combining its established database business with cloud infrastructure designed for demanding enterprise workflows.

That matters because companies wouldn't want to rebuild their IT systems every time a new AI model arrives. Oracle's database expertise helps here, allowing companies to integrate AI into the systems and data they already rely on without disrupting operations.

title: AI Debt Warning Signs Are Piling Up: Why Bond Markets Are Getting Nervous About AI Infrastructure Spending
detail:
AI Debt Warning Signs Are Piling Up: Why Bond Markets Are Getting Nervous About AI Infrastructure Spending
Johnny Rice, The Motley Fool
Fri, October 16, 2026 at 5:15 PM CDT 4 min read
CRWV
ORCL
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The artificial intelligence (AI) boom has a bit of a problem: someone has to pay for it. Despite soaring sales, the costs are still far ahead of the revenues, and more and more companies are turning to the debt market to fund the gap and continue the AI build-out.

But as companies borrow more to build their data centers and fill them with advanced chips, investors are getting nervous about when they'll see a return -- or if they will. This week, that fear has shown up in the bond market where yields are spiking, and the cost to insure the debt against default has reached record levels for companies like CoreWeave and Oracle.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

CoreWeave's lenders are getting nervous

The turbulence was rough enough for Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to step in to try to reassure investors, telling investors that CoreWeave's "financial strength is improving every day." Despite his insistence, the company's bond prices have plummeted; some were trading around 80% of face value, firmly in "distressed" territory. Rates are spiking too, with its October 2031 bond yield reaching 16%.

Jensen Huang. Image source: Getty Images.

Perhaps the clearest sign of bond investor unease was the jump in the five- year credit default swaps (CDS) spread -- basically the cost to insure CoreWeave debt against default -- which reached a record high of about 1,195 basis points. In simple terms, that means it would cost an investor $119,500 a year to insure $1 million in CoreWeave debt.

Oracle's borrowing comes under scrutiny

While CoreWeave took the brunt of it, Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) was not spared either. On Thursday, its five-year CDS spread was nearing 300 basis points, a record for the company.

Oracle's notes due in November 2032 were yielding 7.24% on Wednesday. This is coming just on the heels of a recent credit rating downgrade from S&P Global, which now rates Oracle just one notch above speculative or "junk" grade.

The unease extends across the AI trade

Bonds tied to Meta's Hyperion data-center project have fallen, trading around 91 cents on the dollar and yields reaching as high as 7.55% as of late September. CDS spreads have reached above 100 basis points.

SoftBank, a major backer of OpenAI and other AI ventures, saw its five-year CDS spread climb 24 basis points to 424 on Thursday. SpaceX saw its debt-insurance costs rise sharply during the week too.

title: Does The Move In Snowflake Stock Change Anything?
detail:
Does The Move In Snowflake Stock Change Anything?
Trefis Team

Image from Pexels

Snowflake (SNOW) stock rose 59.3% from January 18 to October 15, 2026, against 12.5% for the S&P 500. The company reported quarterly results three times along the way, on February 25, May 27 and September 2. Buyers appear to be betting that customers using AI on Snowflake's data platform will keep its sales growth climbing while its losses shrink. So how much faster is Snowflake growing than it was in January?

Snowflake Has Grown Faster Every Quarter Since January

Snowflake's revenue is growing about five percentage points faster than when the rise began. Revenue grew 30.1% from a year earlier in fiscal Q4 2026, the quarter that ended January 31. That pace reached 35.1% in fiscal Q2 2027, with growth registering higher in each quarter along the way. Product revenue, nearly all of Snowflake's sales, grew 37% in that latest quarter. On the September 2 call, management said customers using AI on Snowflake consume more across the data platform.

The stock's two largest one-day gains during the rise came right after the May 27 and September 2 reports. Shares rose 37% on May 28, the day after Snowflake reported fiscal Q1 2027 results. On the September 2 call, management said it had raised its fiscal 2027 forecast for product revenue growth by more than five percentage points, to 36%. The stock gained 16.6% the next day.

A run higher can leave Snowflake a larger share of what you own than you planned. See how to protect a concentrated position.

How Far Have Snowflake's Losses Shrunk?

Snowflake's operating loss came to 17.0% of revenue in fiscal Q2 2027, against 29.7% in fiscal Q2 2026. The company's losses are narrowing, though it still loses money. Management said on the September 2 call that Snowflake remains on track for a profit under standard accounting rules (GAAP) in fiscal Q4 2028.

Yet management also said its fast-growing AI workloads carry a lower margin today. So Snowflake keeps less of each dollar on the sales that are lifting its growth, at least for now.

Why Snowflake Is Still Valued On Its Sales

Snowflake is still valued on its sales because it remains unprofitable, despite the faster growth. It lost $1.09 billion over the twelve months to July 31, 2026, so its price-to-earnings multiple is not meaningful. Its operating loss over those twelve months stood at 22.8% of revenue. That marks the smallest figure at any quarter end from fiscal Q2 2021 on, yet it is still a loss.

On sales, the stock trades at 21.5 times, against 3.1 for the S&P 500. At that multiple, the share price appears to assume that both the faster growth and the shrinking losses continue.

Microsoft Is Spending Heavily To Meet AI Demand

The cost is the AI capacity Microsoft is building, and the company's executives raised it on that same call. Customer demand still exceeds the capacity Microsoft has available, management said. In July, the company expected to spend over $50 billion on capital in fiscal Q1 2027, covering the July to September quarter. This figure includes the effect of a change in how it counts some leases. Microsoft also expects capital spending for fiscal 2027 as a whole to grow from the year before.

That heavy spending already shows in Microsoft's financial results. Gross margin was 67.2% in fiscal Q4 2026, against 68.6% a year earlier. Management attributed this decline to a shift in sales toward Azure and to continued investment in AI infrastructure. Free cash flow, the cash left after that spending, fell to $19.6 billion from $25.6 billion a year earlier, even as cash from operations rose.

Microsoft's Cloud Business And The Price You Pay

Microsoft's Intelligent Cloud segment brought in $39.3 billion in fiscal Q4 2026. This accounted for more than two-fifths of the company's revenue and represented 32% growth from a year earlier. No other Microsoft segment grew as fast during that quarter, and revenue in Azure and other cloud services grew 43%. Microsoft is building capacity to keep up with precisely this growth.

At today's price, there is little room for that spending to disappoint. Microsoft stock trades at 30.0 times its earnings over the past twelve months, against 22.7 for the S&P 500. At the end of June, the same earnings were priced at 20.7 times, the lowest at any quarter end since fiscal 2017. On October 15, the shares closed less than 1% below their highest close of the past year. The current stock price appears to assume the spending will pay off.

How Serious Is The Spending Risk For Microsoft?

Microsoft shareholders face a real but slow risk. Operating margin was 45.1% in fiscal Q4 2026, against 44.9% a year earlier, meaning Microsoft still keeps a slightly larger share of its sales as operating profit. For fiscal 2027 as a whole, management expects operating margin to be down less than 1 point, even as the company invests to meet growing demand.

So far, the cost shows up in Microsoft's cash and its gross margin, while operating margin has held steady. Free cash flow is the key metric to watch in Microsoft's next report, which will cover the July to September quarter.

Our purpose is to inform you with unique data so you make the right investment decisions. That said, betting on a single stock is always risky, no matter which direction you choose.
